abstract: We consider polynomial-time computation over arbitrary structures, with unit cost for the primitive operations and relations and with nondeterministic witnesses consisting of arbitrary structure elements. We prove that every finite-signature structure with two distinct available elements and containing a binary operation $*$ and total unary operations $L,R$ such that $L(x*y)=x$ and $R(x*y)=y$ satisfies $P\ne NP$. The proof encodes an exponentially long computation in one element. An incorrect transition has a polynomial-size binary address, and hence the existence of an error is an $NBP$ problem. Existence of a correct accepting trace belongs to the mixed second level $\Sigma_2^{S,B}$, with an arbitrary-element existential block followed by a binary universal block. We obtain $EXP\subseteq\Sigma_2^{S,B}\subseteq PH$. A hypothetical equality $P=NP$ would collapse this hierarchy to $P$ and imply $P=EXP$, contradicting a direct deterministic diagonalization over the same structure. A simulation by function graphs extends the obstruction to every jointly injective binary primitive under the same assumptions on equality and available elements. Consequently no unary predicate on Malcev's free binary-tree algebra yields $P=NP$, with or without the projections. In contrast, starting from the author's unary example, we construct five infinite structures with binary operations and $P=NP$. These include an algebra with one binary operation and one constant, an expansion with an associative rectangular-band operation, and an algebra with one binary operation whose every row and column has infinite image.
hook: P differs from NP over any structure with a pairing function and projections; other structures have P=NP.
summary: Over structures with a binary operation and two inverse projections, the author proves P is not NP, and gives five infinite structures where P equals NP. The proof encodes exponentially long computations in one element. It concerns computation over abstract structures, not the classical Turing P versus NP question.
title: A negative answer to the final question in "Les petits cailloux"
